analysis.one_liner: Requires TV stations to give federal candidates free broadcast time before elections.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one senator with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on August 2, 1990 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every television station to provide free airtime to candidates for President, Vice President, Senate, and House in the 45 days before a general election, with the amount set by the Federal Communications Commission. In exchange, a candidate using the free time would have to give up buying or accepting any other television ads during that window, and use the free time for speeches, interviews, or debates rather than attack commercials. The goal was to reduce how much money campaigns must raise to pay broadcasters for political ads.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates for federal office, who would get guaranteed free television time instead of having to raise large sums to buy ads; voters, who would see more candidates presenting their views directly in speeches, interviews, and debates; and the general public, whose campaigns would be less dependent on donations from big donors to cover broadcast advertising costs.

how_it_helps.text: Each television licensee must make free broadcast time, in an amount set by the FCC, available to legally qualified candidates for President, Vice President, Senate, and House during the 45 days before a general election, scheduled at hours reflecting actual viewing habits.

Candidates receiving the free time must forgo buying or accepting any additional television time in that period, replacing paid political advertising with direct candidate appearances — speeches, interviews, and debates — which reduces the money campaigns must raise.
Stations are barred from censoring the candidates' broadcasts, and the FCC must study how the program works and recommend whether to extend it to primary elections.

analysis.who_pays: Television broadcasters, who would have to give up airtime during valuable viewing hours and lose the revenue from selling political ads during the 45-day window, since the free-time recipients are barred from purchasing additional television advertising.

drawbacks.text: Broadcasters bear a direct financial cost: they must give up paid airtime during peak viewing hours and forgo political advertising revenue in the final 45 days of a campaign, the period when political ad spending is heaviest.

The bill does not actually cap campaign spending or donations — a candidate could still raise and spend unlimited money on other forms of persuasion, such as radio, mail, or direct voter contact, so the effect on the role of money in politics is limited to television.

The FCC would decide how much time each candidate gets and how to treat minor-party candidates, whose allocation could be reduced based on small-dollar contributions received — giving a regulator discretion over who gets broadcast access in elections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real cost of American elections — the enormous sums candidates must raise to buy television ads — by substituting free airtime, a reasonable design since stations use spectrum licensed to serve the public interest. Its limits are real but modest: it applies only to general elections and only to television, so it would not end the broader money chase, and the cost falls on broadcasters in the form of foregone ad revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on August 2, 1990, and it sat there — no hearing, no vote, no action — until Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing it.

narrative.text: Senator William Roth introduced the bill in the Senate on August 2, 1990, near the end of the 101st Congress.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The full action history shows no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Television broadcasters, who kept the political advertising market intact rather than giving up paid airtime in the final 45 days of federal campaigns. No candidate or voter received any benefit, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require free television airtime for federal general-election candidates.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing or markup — for the remaining five months of the Congress.

against.name: Broadcast television industry
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in defeating the bill, which would have taken paid political advertising revenue and forced free candidate airtime on stations; the industry has historically opposed free-airtime mandates.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Stations would have to hand over prime viewing time to candidates at no charge and lose political ad sales during the 45-day window when campaign spending is heaviest, since free-time recipients cannot buy additional TV ads. The industry's revenue from selling election-season ads is the expense candidates would no longer have to pass on to their donors.

Television ad buyers and the consultants who profit from producing and placing political ads would lose a large share of general-election television business, since candidates using free time must limit themselves to direct speeches, interviews, and debates rather than commercials.
